source_refs.note: Topic 2.5 with the second Example 2.4 (PDF 33-34, printed 30-31). The example number 2.4 is printed twice in the chapter.

blocks.text: A body falling freely under the action of gravity is the most familiar example of uniformly accelerated rectilinear motion. According to Galileo, all bodies fall freely (in vacuum) under the acceleration due to gravity, denoted by g, whose experimental value is 9.8 m s^-2 in SI units. This means that different bodies, when allowed to fall from the same height, strike the ground with the same velocity. As regards the sign of g, it is taken positive for a falling body (when the initial velocity is zero) and negative for a body projected vertically upward (when the initial velocity is not zero).

blocks.title: Equations of motion for a freely falling body
blocks.text: On putting a = g the equations become vf = vi + gt; S = h = vi t + (1/2) g t^2; vf^2 - vi^2 = 2gh.

blocks.title: Example 2.4
blocks.problem: An iron ball of mass 1 kg is dropped from a tower and reaches the ground in 3.34 s. Find (a) the height of the tower, (b) the velocity of the ball on striking the ground.
steps: The ball falls under gravity, so a = g in the equations of motion; m = 1 kg, t = 3.34 s, vi = 0, vf = ?, a = g = 9.8 m s^-2. (a) Using the first equation, vf = vi + gt = 0 + (9.8 m s^-2)(3.34 s) = 32.7 m s^-1. (b) The velocity of the ball on striking the ground can be determined by using the third equation: vf^2 - vi^2 = 2gh, (32.7 m s^-1)^2 - 0 = 2 x 9.8 m s^-2 x h, h = 1069.29 m^2 s^-2 / 19.6 m s^-2 = 54.56 m.
book_errors: (b) The velocity of the ball on striking the ground can be determined

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The question asks for (a) the height and (b) the velocity, but the solution labels the velocity (a) and the height (b). The velocity 32.7 m s^-1 answers part (b) and the height 54.56 m answers part (a); the working is right.
